steps.title: Linear search
steps.content: Linear search checks items one by one until the target is found or the list ends. It works on sorted and unsorted data.
steps.example: Find 8 in [4,2,8,6]: inspect 4, then 2, then 8. Three comparisons.

steps.title: Count linear comparisons
steps.prompt: In the array [3,6,9,12,15], how many checks are needed to find 12 with a left-to-right linear search?

steps.title: Binary search halves the range
steps.content: Binary search requires sorted data. Compare the target with the middle value, discard the half that cannot contain it, then repeat.
steps.example: Search 7 in [1,3,5,7,9]. Middle is 5; search the right half [7,9], then find 7.
steps.tip: Never apply ordinary binary search to an unsorted array.

steps.title: Choose the complexity
steps.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
steps.explanation: Each comparison cuts the remaining search interval roughly in half, so O(log n).

steps.title: Know the trade-off
steps.content: Linear search needs no sorting and is simple for tiny lists. Binary search is faster for large sorted data, but the ordering requirement must be satisfied.

questions.prompt: Which search works on an unsorted array?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks every item and does not require sorting.

questions.prompt: What prerequisite does binary search have?
options: The array must contain unique values
The array must have even length
questions.explanation: Binary search relies on order to discard half the remaining range.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
questions.explanation: The target may be last or absent, requiring n checks.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search?
questions.explanation: The search range halves at each iteration.

questions.prompt: When is linear search a reasonable choice?
questions.explanation: Linear search is simple and does not need preprocessing or sorted input.
